content: 1. A multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted and published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016, focusing on patterns of HIV-1 drug resistance following first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) failure in six sub-Saharan African countries. The findings have significant implications for second-line ART strategies. 2. Hamers RL, Sigaloff KC, Wensing AM, Wallis CL, Kityo C, Siwale M, and colleagues analyzed HIV-1 drug resistance patterns after first-line ART failure in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012, highlights the importance of tailoring second-line ART regimens based on resistance profiles. 3. Ford N, Orrell C, Shubber Z, Apollo T, and Vojnov L conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on HIV viral resuppression following elevated viral loads. Their findings, published in The Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2019, emphasize the potential for viral suppression with appropriate interventions. 4. Phillips A, Bansi-Matharu L, Cambiano V, and the HIV Modelling Consortium evaluated modifications in viral load monitoring in sub-Saharan Africa. Their modeling study, published in 2021, informed WHO guidance on optimizing monitoring strategies. 5. The WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring provide comprehensive recommendations for improving HIV care globally. 6. Shroufi A, Van Cutsem G, Cambiano V, Bansi-Matharu L, Duncan K, Murphy RA, and colleagues explored the feasibility of simplifying the switch to second-line ART in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study, published in AIDS in 2019, assessed the use of a single viral load measurement to define efavirenz-based first-line failure. 7. Villa G, Abdullahi A, Owusu D, Smith C, Azumah M, Sayeed L, and colleagues investigated the use of point-of-care viral load testing to determine virological suppression and resuppression in HIV care settings in sub-Saharan Africa. Their findings were published in EClinicalMedicine in 2020. 8. The WHO HIV molecular diagnostics toolkit aims to improve access to viral load testing and early infant diagnosis, addressing critical gaps in HIV care. 9. Luo R, Boeras D, Broyles L, and Vojnov L conducted a systematic review on the HIV viral load threshold for treatment failure. Their findings, included in updated WHO recommendations, highlight the impact of thresholds on disease progression, drug resistance, and HIV transmission. 10. Mofenson L reviewed mother-to-child transmission of HIV, providing unpublished insights into prevention strategies. 11. Médecins Sans Frontières published a report in 2016 on the successes and challenges of implementing routine HIV viral load monitoring, emphasizing the need for sustainable solutions. 12. Vojnov L, Fong Y, Prescott M, Ford N, Carmona S, Zeh C, and colleagues conducted a meta-analysis on the use of dried blood spots for viral load testing. Their findings, included in WHO recommendations, support the use of this method for improving access to testing. 13. The WHO's programmatic update on HIV diagnosis and antiretroviral use in HIV-exposed infants provides guidance on improving care for this vulnerable population. 14. The Clinton Health Access Initiative's 2020 HIV market report highlights the state of the HIV market in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing the need for equitable access to treatment. 15. The WHO's list of prequalified in vitro diagnostic products ensures the quality and reliability of diagnostic tools for HIV care. 16. Le Roux S, Meyer L, and Vojnov L conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing point-of-care and laboratory-based nucleic acid testing for routine HIV viral load monitoring. Their findings, included in WHO recommendations, highlight the clinical and operational benefits of point-of-care testing. 17. Drain PK, Dorward J, Violette LR, Quame-Amaglo J, Thomas KK, Samsunder N, and colleagues evaluated the STREAM trial, which combined point-of-care HIV viral load testing with task shifting to improve treatment outcomes. Their findings were published in The Lancet HIV in 2020. 18. Boeke CE, Joseph J, Atem C, Banda C, Coulibaly KD, Doi N, and colleagues assessed the implementation of near point-of-care viral load testing in public health facilities across seven sub-Saharan African countries. Their study was published in The Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2021. 19. Ndlovu Z, Fajardo E, Mbofana E, Maparo T, Garone D, Metcalf C, and colleagues conducted a feasibility study on multidisease testing for HIV and TB using the GeneXpert platform in rural Zimbabwe. Their findings were published in PLOS One in 2018. 20. Mangone E, Cintron C, Haider R, Johns B, Avila C, Vartanova Y, and colleagues analyzed the cost-effectiveness of nationally scaled point-of-care diagnostic platforms compared to central laboratory models for routine HIV viral load monitoring in Kenya. Their findings were presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in 2018. 21. De Necker M, de Beer JC, Stander MP, Connell CD, and Mwai D modeled the economic and public health impact of decentralized HIV viral load testing in Kenya. Their study was published in PLOS One in 2019. 22. Girdwood SJ, Crompton T, Sharma M, Dorward J, Garrett N, Drain PK, and colleagues evaluated the cost-effectiveness of adoption strategies for point-of-care HIV viral load monitoring in South Africa. Their findings were published in EClinicalMedicine in 2020. 23. Bwana P, Ageng’o J, and Mwau M assessed the performance and usability of the Cepheid GeneXpert HIV-1 qualitative and quantitative assay in Kenya. Their study was published in PLOS One in 2019. 24. Mariani D, de Azevedo M, Vasconcellos I, Ribeiro L, Alves C, Ferreira OC Jr., and colleagues evaluated the performance of a new point-of-care HIV viral load technology to identify patients failing antiretroviral treatment. Their findings were published in The Journal of Clinical Virology in 2020. 25. Cepheid’s High Burden Developing Country (HBDC) program aims to improve global access to diagnostic tools for HIV care. 26. Silva DS explored ethical and equity considerations regarding the potential future implementation of novel HIV/AIDS diagnostics. Their findings were included in updated WHO recommendations. 27. Rutherford GW, Anglemyer A, Easterbrook PJ, Horvath T, Vitoria M, Penazzato M, and colleagues systematically reviewed the performance of the 2010 WHO immunologic and clinical criteria for predicting virologic failure in adults and children on ART. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2014. 28. Chow EP, Read TR, Chen MY, Fehler G, Bradshaw CS, Fairley CK, and colleagues demonstrated that routine CD4 cell count monitoring rarely contributes to clinical decision-making in virologically suppressed HIV-infected patients on ART. Their study was published in HIV Medicine in 2015. 29. Hyle EP, Sax PE, and Walensky RP evaluated the potential cost savings of reduced CD4 monitoring in stable HIV patients receiving ART. Their findings were published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2013. 30. Duncan CJ, Schmid ML, Schwab U, Price DA, and Ong E highlighted the futility of CD4+ monitoring in HIV-1 patients with CD4+ cell counts above 350 cells/µL on suppressive ART. Their study was published in AIDS in 2014. 31. The WHO supports the use of dried blood spot samples for HIV-1 viral load testing with most currently available technologies, as demonstrated in a pooled meta-analysis and systematic review. 32. Phillips A, Shroufi A, Vojnov L, Cohn J, Roberts T, Ellman T, and colleagues emphasized the importance of viral load-informed differentiated care for sustainable HIV treatment in Africa. Their findings were published in Nature in 2015.
